en: The Jātaka:
The Collection of Ten,
Chapter on the Four Gates (Catudvāravagga)
14. The Bhūripañña Jātaka “It is true indeed, O Bhūripañña,
that you possess such glory, steadfastness, and wisdom as these!”
"One who eats barley with little sauce does not protect the wealth brought by his own being.
"Bringing happiness to maturity through suffering..."
Seeking the right time at the right time, shrouded by zeal,
he opens the doors to the goal;
therefore, I am satisfied even with this rice and gruel.
Having known the right time for exertion,
and having matured the goal through wise counsels,
I shall stretch out my limbs like the yawnings of a lion.
“By means of that psychic power, you shall see me once again.
Some do not commit evil even when happy,
while others refrain out of fear of blame and social disapproval.
“Being so powerful and contemplating such vast wealth,
for what reason do you not cause me suffering?
“The wise do not act for the sake of their own pleasure.”
They perform evil deeds;
though touched by suffering and even faltering,
they do not abandon their nature due to desire and hatred.
“By whatever means possible,
whether gentle or harsh,
one should uplift one’s own distressed self.”
“Later, one should practice the Dhamma.
“Under the shade of whichever tree one might sit or lie down, [that tree]...”
One should not break its branch,
for that evil person is a betrayer of friends.
Even toward one from whom a man may learn the Dhamma...
Those virtuous ones who dispel his doubt—
for them he has both an island and a refuge;
a wise person should not let friendship with such a one decay.”
“A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good;
one who has gone forth but is unrestrained is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good.”
It is not good for a wise man to be angry.
A Kshatriya, a lord of the earth, should act with reflection, not without reflection.
“O King, for those who act with circumspection, fame and renown increase.
The Fourteenth Jātaka: Bhūripañña (The Great Wisdom).
